by Mimi Billing

Good morning Luca,



Stockholm has been buzzing this week with the annual Tech Arena event, drawing around 12k attendees over two days.



Hosted in a vast arena usually reserved for soccer, ice hockey and concerts, the event featured partnership booths, coffee stations, three stages and dedicated areas for matchmaking, media and investors.



Tech Arena is often described as the Swedish answer to the Finnish tech conference Slush, but beyond the similarly dim lighting, it’s a very different affair. Despite strong stage appearances from Mistral’s Arthur Mensch, Lovable’s co-founder Fabian Hedin and Station F’s Roxanne Varza, plus a pitch competition, startups are only a small part of the program.



The event is just as much a platform for corporates and partners to showcase themselves. In honour of Zlatan Ibrahimović’s appearance, Vanta set up a soccer goal. Nordea handed out free ice cream, while Deutsche Telekom served a mix of German and Swedish fika.



As many tech event organisers know, it’s hard to keep scaleup founders on the conference floor. After their talks, Kry founder Johannes Schildt and Voi founder Fredrik Hjelm quickly disappeared, heading either back into the city or to the speakers’ lounge. Nor were many other high-profile founders lingering.



While VCs praised the dedicated investor day held ahead of the conference, some international VCs seemed underwhelmed by the scope of the main event. “Slush is much better,” one investor told me.



And yes, Slush is known to host a great gathering. But perhaps the ecosystem also needs events like this: spaces where politicians, corporates like Meta, banks, national organisations, service providers, investors, and startups all converge to “share ideas” — which appears to be the true focus here.



Last year, I felt Tech Arena lacked a clear identity. Now, I’m starting to think this breadth is its identity.



And personally, I appreciated drifting between the media zone, gossipy backstage conversations on big tech versus startups, and unexpected reunions with people I hadn’t seen in years.



Slush already exists. So why compete — when you can build something entirely different?
